data:
This section explains how PULSE is put together. Read it before you change a deployment or build against the API.
Sovereign inferenceOne shared model server, time budgets, and grounding. The judging ladderHow PULSE withholds proposals its own judge disagrees with. Agent activityThe live card that shows what every agent is doing.
data.a-diagnosis-fills-the-rest-of-the-app#A:
When GenerateDiagnostic finishes, PULSE copies the structured findings into the tables the other screens read. This step makes no extra model calls and invents nothing. It runs once per diagnosis.
Finding Becomes The 4-week plan (cronogram) A 30-day follow-up cycle with one planner task per entry Channel prescription suggestions Draft content, pending review, on the Approval screen Prescriptions and audience segments One draft campaign linked to the diagnosis Audience segments One Customer 360 profile per segment Competitive and positioning analysis A market summary on the Radar In the background, PULSE also runs market research for the niche and prospects the public web for up to five leads.
data.background-workers#Background workers:
serve starts these loops alongside the API:
Worker What it does Social engine Daily. Drafts LinkedIn, X, and Instagram copy for each active campaign, for review. When the blog channel is armed, it also drafts and schedules one blog post per campaign. Publishing worker Every 30 seconds. Dispatches scheduled posts that are due. Podcast, audiobook, and shorts engines Generate episodes and videos for active campaigns and stage them. The shorts engine refuses to start when the image has no video tool. Document engine Daily. Generates documents for active campaigns. Predictive churn engine Daily. Scores synced HubSpot leads for churn risk and schedules retention tasks. Site audit engine Daily at 03:47 UTC. Audits one configured site and files a digest. See Site pipeline. Self-healing loop Watches local resources and the inference endpoints. Read it with SelfHealService/GetStatus. Nothing a worker drafts is published unless the channel is armed. See Publishing controls.
data.every-call-goes-through-the-same-chain#E:
gRPC calls pass through the same interceptors in the same order:
Panic recovery. Optional per-caller rate limiting, keyed by peer IP. It is off unless PULSE_RATE_RPS is set. Request logging. Authentication. Every method needs a valid bearer token, except IdentityService/Login, ModelService/GetModelStatus, and reflection. When a licence file is configured and invalid or expired, calls are refused with license expired or invalid. Streaming calls also get serialized sends and a heartbeat. The heartbeat keeps long generations alive through proxies while the model is still thinking.
data.one-process-one-port#One process, one po:
pulse-server serve is one Go process listening on one port. A multiplexer (cmux) splits that port in two:
Connections with content-type: application/grpc go to the gRPC server. Everything else goes to an HTTP handler. It serves gRPC-Web for browsers, /health, generated media, the voice endpoints, sign-in helpers, the podcast feed, the A2A agent card, and, when PULSE_WEB_DIR is set, the Flutter web build itself. When the backend serves the web build, the app and the API share an origin and browsers never make CORS requests.
data.the-services#The services:
The backend registers these gRPC services. Each one is documented in the API reference.
Area Services Analysis DiagnosticService, RadarService, InsightsService, Customer360Service Content ContentService, StudioService, AvatarService, CourseService, PublishingService Campaigns and results CampaignService, MetricsService, AnalyticsService, FollowUpService Leads and accounts LeadService, IntegrationService, InfluencerService AI ModelService, TwinService, ActivityService Platform IdentityService, ConfigService, SelfHealService, MeteringService (deprecated) Shared ui components BillingService, ConnectionsService, RunnersService, ProfileService, AccessService
data.where-data-lives#Where data lives: SQLite holds the business data: diagnostics, content, campaigns, leads, and more. In a cluster, Litestream replicates it to the in-cluster object store. SQLite has one writer, so a deployment runs one backend instance. OAuth tokens in the integrations table are sealed column by column before they are written. The rest of the database file is not encrypted. The appfs root holds sessions, generated media, and the memo cache, each sealed. It uses the object store when one is configured, or a sealed local directory otherwise. The server will not start if it cannot mount it. The Litestream replica is plaintext at rest, including password hashes. The Litestream version in use cannot encrypt it, and the fix is an open owner decision. See the comments in grpc/litestream.yml.

data: A long generation can hold the inference server for minutes. Without a shared view, it is visible only on the screen that started it. The agent activity card fixes that. It is fed by ActivityService.SubscribeAgentActivity.
data.opening-the-page-mid-run#Opening the pag: When you subscribe, the server first replays every run in progress, with the steps recorded so far. Then it sends snapshot_complete, and after that live events. So a page opened halfway through a run still shows that run.
data.the-featured-strip#The featured strip: ActivityService.ListFeaturedMessages returns operator-written sponsor and partner cards for the rotating strip. The server reads them from a file named by FEATURED_MESSAGES_PATH. When that is unset, it looks for a file named featured_messages.json in /app, the working directory, data, and /app/data, in that order. No file means an empty strip, not an error. You can change the cards without rebuilding the app.
data.what-you-see#What you see:
Each run shows its agent (for example pulse:whitepaper), its status (running, done, or failed), and its steps. PULSE has no multi-step reasoning loop, so one generation is usually one step. The useful parts are the model, the token count, and the latency.
A step can also carry provenance: whether the answer is fresh or reused from a cache, and whether it was produced in a degraded mode. A healthy, fresh answer shows nothing extra. The card calls out only reused, offline, or degraded answers.
data.whose-runs-you-see#Whose runs you see:
By default you see your own session’s runs. The server uses the session field of the request, or, when that is empty, the caller’s x-agent-trace-id header.
Work started without a request behind it (a schedule, a WhatsApp message, an A2A call, a background engine) has no session. A scoped subscriber does not see those runs. Only a subscriber that sends neither a session nor a trace ID gets the ambient view of everything. An operator console does that on purpose.

data: PULSE’s agents propose. Before some proposals are saved or shown, a judge checks each one against the evidence the run actually gathered. This is the judging ladder, from the shared inference/judgement library, with the wire format from ui/judgement. It runs inside the PULSE process.
data.turning-it-off#Turning it off: Set PULSE_JUDGEMENT=off. Every proposal then passes unjudged, and the judgement fields are unset.
data.what-is-judged#What is judged: Proposal Where it appears Channel prescriptions Diagnostic.channel_prescriptions Brand-visibility insights Diagnostic.brand_visibility Content gaps ContentGapsResponse.gaps Content pillars ContentStrategyResponse.pillars Roadmap phases StrategyRoadmapResponse.phases The evidence is what that run collected: your intake answers, the scraped website, web research, Google Analytics and Google Ads signals, and the latest diagnosis findings.
data.what-the-verdict-does#What the verdict d:
Verdict Effect Concur The proposal is kept, with its verdict attached. Unable to judge The proposal is kept and marked. Dissent The proposal is withheld. It appears only in the response’s judgements set, with accepted=false. A withheld prescription never becomes a draft or a scheduled post, because the diagnosis fans out only what was kept.
Each judged message carries a judgement field, and each response carries a judgements set that lists every verdict (accepted and rejected) with the judge’s counts. Any verdict fields the model wrote itself are stripped from its output first. The judge is the only source of a verdict.

data: Every AI feature in PULSE runs on the Runink platform’s own inference server: mistral.rs’s mistralrs-server. PULSE sends no prompt, no customer data, and no generated text to any third-party model API.
data.grounding#Grounding:
Generators ground their output in real sources before they write:
Web research. A headless Chrome scraper and extractor (internal/metasearch) reads live pages and search results. The diagnosis reads your website this way. The retrieval corpus. A per-tenant vector and keyword index (store/corpus). PULSE embeds text by calling /v1/embeddings at EMBEDDING_URL. EMBEDDING_FORMAT names the embedding model’s instruction format. Unset means qwen3-embedding. The other accepted values are nomic-v1.5 and raw. An unknown value stops the server at startup. When the embedding endpoint is unreachable, the generators still run, but they say they are ungrounded rather than invent facts. The startup log states grounding ACTIVE or grounding INACTIVE: .
data.is-the-model-ready#Is the model ready:
Two signals report readiness, and both use the same test: the engine process is running, and a readiness check against the engine has confirmed it can serve a request.
GET /health returns model_ready. ModelService/GetModelStatus returns ready. The app polls it on startup. A process that has started but is still loading weights counts as not ready.
data.one-server-for-everything#One server for:
All AI services share one inference server and one model server object inside PULSE, so they share one set of agent prompts and parameters (agents/pulse.ini and the templates in agents/templates/).
The backend finds the server one of two ways:
Remote. When INFERENCE_REMOTE_URL is set, PULSE uses the shared inference plane at that address and starts nothing itself. Local. Otherwise it starts mistralrs-server as a child process. Speech-to-text works the same way with its own variable, VOXTRAL_REMOTE_URL, and its own mistralrs-server serving Voxtral. Text-to-speech is Runink TIDE’s shared ttsd service, reached through TTSD_URL (unset: the in-cluster Service; empty: voice output off). PULSE embeds no speech engine.
Both servers start in the background. If a binary or model is missing, PULSE still starts, and AI calls fail with inference server is not running instead of blocking the whole app.
data.output-guards#Output guards: The output of content agents is screened before it reaches you. Other agents (diagnostics, radar, the assistant) stream straight through by default. To screen them too, set PULSE_EGRESS_ALL_AGENTS. It is opt-in because screening buffers the whole response, so you lose token-by-token streaming.
data.repeat-requests#Repeat requests: An exact repeat of a content generation is served from a cache instead of running the model again. PULSE_DEDUP_TTL sets how long an entry lives, as a Go duration. The default is 1h.
data.sharing-the-slot-fairly#Sharing the slot:
Optional admission control queues or refuses work when the model is busy. It is off unless PULSE_ADMIT_MAX is above zero.
Variable Meaning PULSE_ADMIT_MAX Maximum concurrent inference calls. 0 turns admission off. PULSE_ADMIT_QUEUE Maximum waiters before backpressure. 0 is unbounded. PULSE_ADMIT_MODE reject (default) or degrade. PULSE_ADMIT_WEIGHTS Scheduling weights keyed by the x-subscription-tier request metadata, for example enterprise:4,dedicated:4,lite:1. A request without that metadata is scheduled as default. When the pool is full in reject mode, the caller gets ResourceExhausted: the inference plane is at capacity and declined this request; nothing was generated — retry in a few minutes.
data.time-budgets#Time budgets:
The model runs on CPU and one generation can take many minutes. PULSE gives each generation two clocks:
Clock Default Override Wait for the first token (queue plus prompt processing) 5 minutes PULSE_FIRST_TOKEN_SECONDS Decode Sized from the agent’s token budget and the platform decode rate, capped at 45 minutes PULSE_GENERATION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS The decode rate comes from INFERENCE_DECODE_TOK_S, which TIDE injects. If a budget is too short to produce an answer that parses, PULSE refuses up front and sends nothing to the model. The error says so and names PULSE_GENERATION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS.
data.which-model#Which model:
INFERENCE_MODEL names the model PULSE asks the server for. Set it explicitly to the general model your inference server loads: on Runink Server that is Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen, Apache-2.0). When it is unset, PULSE falls back to a legacy default that current servers do not load. Every agent uses this one model today; see Model cards.
INFERENCE_MODEL must match what the server actually loads. PULSE does not check. If they disagree, the backend asks for a model the server never loaded. The old LLAMA_* variable names are no longer read at all.

data:
This guide is for people changing PULSE or building against its API.
Calling the APIgrpcurl, bearer tokens, streaming, gRPC-Web, and A2A. API referenceEvery service, method, and message.
data.build-and-test#Build and test:
The backend builds only with the sibling repositories checked out next to pulse/: inference, security, mesh, store, ui, and billing.
cd grpc && go build -o bin/pulse-server . cd grpc && go test ./... cd grpc && go vet ./... cd flutter && flutter analyze Sibling checkouts may be on another branch. To build against a specific sibling version, add a worktree of it and point a GOWORK file outside the repository at it. Don’t switch the shared checkout. To run the backend, see Run PULSE locally.
data.licence-rules-for-contributions#Licence:
PULSE is proprietary.
New files start with an SPDX header: SPDX-License-Identifier: LicenseRef-Runink-Proprietary. After a dependency change, run scripts/gen-third-party-notices.sh. CI fails on stale notices and on disallowed licences. Release builds stay hardened: Go -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w", Flutter web --no-source-maps.
data.regenerate-the-protobuf-code#Regenerate:
Run both commands from the repository root, and always pass the grpc/api/proto input:
buf generate grpc/api/proto --template grpc/buf.gen.yaml -o grpc # Go buf generate grpc/api/proto --template grpc/buf.gen.dart.yaml # Dart, no -o The Go run needs -o grpc, or the code lands at the repository root. The first command does not generate Dart, and nothing tells you. Skip the second and the app compiles against the old messages, and a new field reads as null on the client. Running buf from inside grpc/ picks up a competing buf.yaml and breaks import resolution. Codegen uses local plugins on your PATH: protoc-gen-go, protoc-gen-go-grpc, and protoc-gen-dart. When ui changes judgement.proto, copy it again into proto-vendor/. grpc/cmd/judgement_vendored_test.go fails until you do.
data.repository-layout#Repository layout: Path What it holds grpc/ The Go backend, module github.com/org-runink/pulse (Go 1.26) grpc/main.go, grpc/cmd/ The Cobra entry point and every service. cmd/serve.go wires everything together. grpc/api/proto/pulse/v1/ The .proto files: pulse.proto, activity.proto, commons.proto grpc/api/proto-vendor/ A verbatim copy of runink/ui/judgement/v1/judgement.proto, resolved but never generated grpc/api/v1/ Generated Go code, committed grpc/internal/ ai, db, scoring, apply, metasearch, openbias, forecast, connector clients (hubspot, github, googleanalytics, googleads, spotify), telephony, voice, webrtc, and more grpc/agents/ Agent parameters (pulse.ini), prompt templates, and guardrail rules flutter/lib/ The Flutter app: core/ (gRPC channel, generated stubs, cache, theme) and features/ (one folder per screen) website/ This documentation site The platform pieces are not here. Self-healing, the event mesh, secrets and PKI, the object store, the inference engine, the operator, and infrastructure code live in Runink TIDE or in the extracted libraries. Never add them to this repository.
data.shared-ui-components#Shared UI component: Pages that more than one Runink app shows come from org-runink/ui: design tokens and transport (foundation), billing, datasources, profile, and access. PULSE mounts the Go handler with its own hooks and depends on the Flutter package by path. To try an unmerged ui branch, use a private GOWORK and a gitignored flutter/pubspec_overrides.yaml.
data.the-apps-backend-address#The app\u0026rs: The Flutter client reads PULSE_BACKEND_URL from a --dart-define, default http://localhost:50051. The web build bakes it in at compile time.

data: PULSE’s API is gRPC, package pulse.v1, plus the shared runink.ui.*.v1 services. There is no REST or JSON API for business data.
data.a2a-calling-pulse-from-another-agent#A2A:
PULSE publishes itself as an Agent2Agent (A2A) agent for FACE and the Runink TIDE fleet:
Discovery: GET /.well-known/agent-card.json. Calls: JSON-RPC at /a2a, with a PULSE session as a bearer token in the Authorization header. Calls without a valid session are refused. Choose a persona with the message metadata key skill. The default is market-analyst.
Skill Persona market-analyst Diagnostics, SWOT, positioning content-creator Channel content copywriter Long-form content and whitepapers strategy-agent Prescriptive 30-day plans radar-agent Trend and profile research
data.authenticate#Authenticate:
Call IdentityService/Login with a username and password. The token is in accessToken:
TOK=$(grpcurl -plaintext -d '{"username":"admin","password":""}' \ localhost:52000 pulse.v1.IdentityService/Login | jq -r '.accessToken') Send it on every other call:
grpcurl -plaintext -H "authorization: Bearer $TOK" -d '{}' \ localhost:52000 pulse.v1.CampaignService/ListCampaigns Only three things work without a token: IdentityService/Login, ModelService/GetModelStatus, and reflection (when it is turned on).
Refresh a session at POST /auth/refresh. See HTTP endpoints.
data.discover-the-schema#Discover the schema:
With PULSE_GRPC_REFLECTION=true on a local server:
grpcurl -plaintext localhost:52000 list grpcurl -plaintext localhost:52000 describe pulse.v1.LeadService Reflection is off by default and must stay off on deployed instances. Without it, use the .proto files in grpc/api/proto/pulse/v1/.
data.errors#Errors:
PULSE uses standard gRPC codes and puts a sentence meant for a person in the message. Common ones:
Code Typical cause Unauthenticated Missing, expired, or revoked token PermissionDenied Licence invalid, or your role does not allow the call FailedPrecondition Something must be set up first, for example a HubSpot connection or PULSE_APPLY_ENABLED InvalidArgument A required field is missing or has a bad value ResourceExhausted Rate limit, or the inference plane is at capacity Unavailable A dependency failed: HubSpot, GA4, speech synthesis, media storage Unimplemented The feature does not exist in this deployment, for example still-image generation See Troubleshooting for specific messages.
data.streaming-calls#Streaming calls:
Every AI generator is a server-streaming RPC that returns stream StreamChunk:
Field Meaning text The next piece of output. May be empty. is_final True on the last chunk section A section marker, for example positioning, swot, or grounding progress 0.0 to 1.0 metadata Extra key-value data agent_tasks Actions the backend actually performed, such as a scrape. These are recorded facts, not model claims. A chunk with tasks may have no text. Long generations can go quiet while the model thinks. The server sends heartbeat frames on streams so proxies do not drop them. Use a generous deadline: a long document can take tens of minutes on CPU.
When the model is busy and admission control is on, a call can fail with ResourceExhausted. Retry after a few minutes.
data.tie-runs-to-your-screen#Tie runs to your: Set x-agent-trace-id on your calls, and send the same value as session in ActivityService/SubscribeAgentActivity. Then the activity stream shows only the runs your client started. See Agent activity.
data.transports#Transports:
Everything is on one port.
Client How it connects Native gRPC (Go, grpcurl, the Linux and Android app) HTTP/2 with content-type: application/grpc Browsers gRPC-Web over the same port For browsers served from another origin, the origin must be listed in CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS. The allowed request headers include Authorization, X-Grpc-Web, grpc-timeout, x-agent-trace-id, and x-idempotency-key.

data: This page takes you from a sign-in screen to your first finished Site Audit. It assumes someone has already deployed PULSE for you. To run it on your own machine instead, start with Run PULSE locally.
data.connect-your-accounts-optional#Connect y:
Open System → Integrations. It has two tabs:
Accounts: LinkedIn, Instagram, Google Ads, and Google Analytics. Data sources: HubSpot and GitHub. You can run an audit without any of these. Leads sync needs HubSpot. The forecasts need Google Analytics. Publishing to your website needs GitHub. See Connections.
data.next#Next: Signing in Run PULSE locally User guide
data.review-what-the-audit-produced#Review wh:
A finished diagnosis fills in the rest of the app, with no extra model calls:
Content → Approval holds draft posts, one set per recommended channel. Content → Campaigns holds one draft campaign linked to the diagnosis. Audience → Follow-up holds a 30-day cycle built from the diagnosis’s 4-week plan. Audience → Customer 360 holds one profile per audience segment. Approve or reject the drafts. Nothing leaves PULSE until an administrator has armed publishing. See Publishing controls.
AI steps are slow on CPU. A long generation holds the one shared inference slot for minutes, and other requests wait behind it. The agent activity card shows what is running. See Agent activity.
data.run-a-site-audit#Run a Site Audit:
Open Overview → Site Audit. Enter your website URL. You can add a LinkedIn URL and an Instagram handle, and pick the goals you care about. Then choose Run Site Audit.
The diagnosis streams in as it is written. The site must be reachable, because PULSE reads the live page before it writes anything. See Site Audit.
data.set-your-business-profile#Set your busin: Open System → Settings. Fill in the business name, industry, and timezone. Then set the default content language, the default tone, and your active channels. The app saves these with ConfigService.UpdateConfig. See Business profile.
data.sign-in#Sign in:
Open the PULSE app. Until you sign in, every route redirects to /login.
The login screen asks the backend which methods are on (GET /auth/config) and shows up to two:
Sign in with Google appears only when the deployment has a Google OAuth client configured. Username and password appears unless the deployment has turned on Google-only sign-in. Details, including how accounts get their roles, are in Signing in.

data: There are two ways to run PULSE on your own machine. The Runink TIDE loop runs the whole stack: backend, inference, and the Flutter web app. The direct binary runs only the backend, which is enough to drive and test every non-AI RPC.
data.build#Build:
Generated protobuf code is committed under grpc/api/, so you do not need to run buf to build.
cd grpc && go build -o bin/pulse-server . && cd ..
data.option-1-the-tide-loop#Option 1: the TID:
From your TIDE checkout (the core directory):
cd ../core/grpc # TIDE's Go module; set PULSE_REPO to an absolute path for `dev up` PULSE_REPO=/abs/path/to/pulse go run ./cmd/core dev up pulse This builds the backend and starts it on a free port. It starts the shared inference server when the model weights are present, then builds and serves the Flutter web app pointed at the backend’s real port. TIDE provisions the inference binaries and weights under ../core/artifacts/. TIDE’s CLI is now called tide; core still works as an alias, so these commands are unchanged.
data.prerequisites#Prerequisites: Go 1.26 (see grpc/go.mod). Flutter, for the client. The sibling repositories checked out next to pulse/: core, inference, security, mesh, store, ui, and billing. The backend does not build without them, because grpc/go.mod points at them with replace directives. grpcurl, to call the API by hand.
data.run-the-flutter-client#Run the Flutter c: cd flutter flutter run -d chrome # web flutter run -d linux # desktop flutter run # a connected Android device The client reads its backend address from PULSE_BACKEND_URL, a --dart-define that defaults to http://localhost:50051. For the web build it is fixed at compile time, which is why core dev up rebuilds the bundle when the backend port changes.
data.run-the-tests#Run the tests: cd grpc && go test ./... cd flutter && flutter analyze
data.sign-in-and-call-an-rpc#Sign in and call:
TOK=$(grpcurl -plaintext -d '{"username":"admin","password":""}' \ localhost:52000 pulse.v1.IdentityService/Login | jq -r '.accessToken') grpcurl -plaintext -H "authorization: Bearer $TOK" -d '{}' \ localhost:52000 pulse.v1.CampaignService/ListCampaigns The token is in the accessToken field. The repository also ships a smoke driver that runs health, login, whoami, and list calls in one go:
PULSE_PASSWORD='' go run .claude/skills/run-pulse/smoke.go 52000
data.start-the-server#Start the server:
cd grpc PULSE_ADMIN_PASSWORD='' \ PULSE_JWT_SECRET="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" \ PULSE_GRPC_REFLECTION=true \ ./bin/pulse-server serve --port 52000 > /tmp/pulse.log 2>&1 & Three variables matter here:
PULSE_JWT_SECRET is required. Without it serve exits with refusing to start: no session signing key configured. Any value you generate works locally. It must never be a value that has been committed to a repository. PULSE_ADMIN_PASSWORD seeds a break-glass admin with username admin. Without it the log says skipping admin seed; break-glass login unavailable, and every login fails. PULSE_GRPC_REFLECTION=true turns on gRPC server reflection so grpcurl can list services. It is off by default. Never set it on a deployed instance. With no --port (and no PORT variable), the server picks a free port.
Don’t stop the server with pkill -f 'pulse-server serve'. That pattern also matches the shell running the command, so it kills your own command and looks like a server crash. Kill the process by its PID instead.
data.wait-for-health#Wait for health: until curl -s localhost:52000/health | grep -q '"status":"ok"'; do sleep 2; done curl -s localhost:52000/health The response looks like {"status":"ok","model_ready":false,"port":52000}. model_ready stays false until an inference server has loaded its weights. The HTTP status is always 200. PULSE serves every non-AI feature without a model.
data.without-a-model#Without a model: A bare machine has no mistralrs-server and no model weights. The server still starts and serves login, every read, and every create or update. AI calls fail with inference server is not running. That is the expected result, not a bug.

data: PULSE has two ways in: a username and password, and Google sign-in. Both end the same way. The backend returns an access token and a refresh token, and the app sends the access token as a bearer token on every gRPC call.
data.google-sign-in#Google sign-in:
The app posts the Google ID token to POST /auth/google. The backend:
Checks that the token was issued for this deployment’s OAuth client and carries a verified email. Checks the email against the deployment’s allowlist (AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAILS). Google sign-in fails closed. If the allowlist is empty, nobody gets in through Google. Finds your account by email, or creates one with the viewer role on first sign-in. A role the operator granted in advance is kept. If you are not on the allowlist you get this account is not authorized for this instance.
data.how-long-a-session-lasts#How long a sess:
Token Lifetime Access token 24 hours Refresh token 7 days, single use The session behind both At most 30 days from sign-in Each sign-in creates one server-side session. The app exchanges a refresh token at POST /auth/refresh for a new pair in the same session. Each refresh token works once.
Signing out ends the session everywhere it is used. IdentityService.Logout revokes the session, and the access token, the refresh token, and every token refreshed from them stop working at once. On the Account page (click your avatar), you can also end every session on every device.
data.roles#Roles:
Each account has one role, stored on its user row:
Role Granted by admin The break-glass admin account, or an operator grant editor An operator grant (writer or editor) viewer New Google accounts by default, or an operator grant (reader or viewer) Admins see an Admin entry in the navigation. It opens the shared members and roles page, and the server checks your role again on every call there. See Users and access.
data.username-and-password#Username and passw:
The form calls IdentityService.Login with a username and a password. You sign in with your username, not your email address.
A wrong username or password returns invalid credentials, and so does an account that exists but has no usable password (accounts created for Google sign-in get a random, unusable one).
data.which-options-you-see#Which options you:
The login screen reads GET /auth/config, which returns two fields:
Field Meaning google_client_id The public Google OAuth client. Empty means no Sign in with Google button. password_auth false only when the deployment sets AUTH_GOOGLE_ONLY=true. Then the username and password form is hidden.

data: PULSE does its AI work through a small set of agents. Each one has its own instructions, its own limits, and its own guardrails, but they all run on the same model server. A model card says, in plain language, what one agent does, what it reads, what it produces, who checks its work, and where it stops.
data.the-cards#The cards: Agent What you meet it as Diagnostic analyst The written diagnosis from a Site Audit, and the metrics read-out Market radar Radar research, competitor channels, and guest spots Strategy planner Recalculating the route of a 30-day follow-up cycle Channel content creator Posts, emails, outreach drafts, and the shorter Studio pieces Long-form studio Whitepapers, blog posts, and the weekly audiobook Partnership outreach First-contact messages to podcasts, channels, and brands Sales and voice agent Cold-call scripts, live replies on a phone call, and churn watch Customer 360 and journeys Audience profiles, journey maps, content strategy, and roadmaps PULSE assistant The chat on every screen Self-healing operations agent Keeps PULSE’s own services running; the one agent that acts automatically, with an off switch
data.what-every-agent-has-in-common#What ever:
The model. Every agent runs on the same base model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, made by Qwen and released under the Apache-2.0 licence. The deployment decides which model its inference server loads (INFERENCE_MODEL); see Sovereign inference. Runink domain adaptation for these agents is planned; this release uses the base model.
Where it runs. On the deployment’s own inference server: your Runink Server, or the cloud account it runs in. PULSE calls no third-party AI service. Some agents read the public web or your connected accounts while they work, and PULSE talks to the services you connect (HubSpot, LinkedIn, Google Analytics and others) as described in Connections.
Text only. The agents read and write text. The current Server release does not include a vision model, so no agent looks at images or screenshots. Still-image generation is not available, and video needs the video tool the deployment configures. See Content pipeline.
Guardrails before the model. Before any agent is called, PULSE checks the request against a shared rule set. It refuses attempts to override the agent’s instructions, requests to reveal secrets or credentials, requests to reach internal network addresses, and hateful content. Each agent adds its own rules, listed on its card.
Outside text is data, not instructions. Web pages, search results, attached sources, lead and CRM records, inbound customer messages, and call transcripts reach an agent marked as material to read. Before they do, PULSE removes model control codes and hidden characters and takes out text that tries to give the agent instructions. Every agent is told never to follow instructions found in that material.
Value first. Every agent that writes for an audience follows the same brand rule: teach the reader something useful, mention your product at most once and only as an honest example, no hype words, no fake urgency, and end with a real question rather than a hard sell.
People decide. Agents draft, recommend, and score. (The self-healing operations agent is the exception for PULSE’s own infrastructure: it applies a fixed list of safe actions automatically, and an operator can turn that off.) Drafts go to the Approval review queue. A post is published only when a person approved that piece and an administrator armed the channel; rejecting a piece withholds its scheduled posts. The one automatic exception is the reply to an inbound WhatsApp or SMS message from a known contact: it is on by default, passes the same guardrails as every other reply (the message is read as data, injection attempts are refused, the reply is screened), and an administrator can turn it off. See Publishing controls. Some proposals also pass through the judging ladder, and the agent activity card shows every run as it happens.
Evaluation. No published evaluation scores yet, for any agent.

data.guardrails#Guardrails: Value first, no hard sell. The reader’s problem is the subject. Your product appears at most once, as an honest example. No hype words, no fake urgency, and it ends with a real question. Never invents statistics, studies, or customer results. It uses the figures in your brief. Treats lead details, web pages, and search results as material, never as instructions. Refuses unsubstantiated claims such as “100% guaranteed” and deceptive engagement bait. Will not request payments or credentials. Its output is screened before it reaches you, as described in Sovereign inference.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: Content drafts, including the daily campaign drafts and campaign plans, go to the Approval review queue. You edit, approve, or reject each one. A scheduled post goes out only once you approved its content. Rejecting a piece withholds its scheduled posts. Lead outreach drafts are saved on the lead. PULSE does not send them. Nothing is published until an administrator arms the channel. Approval alone does not publish to a disarmed channel. See Publishing controls. A campaign plan is a proposal: creating a campaign does not activate it. Content gaps pass through the judging ladder.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl:
Invented brief and figure.
Brief: audience warehouse supervisors; channel X; figure to use: “re-slotting the top 50 SKUs monthly cut walking time by 18% in a pilot”.
Draft: “Most picking time is walking. Re-slotting your top 50 SKUs every month cut walking time by 18% in one pilot. Which SKUs moved most on your floor last month? #warehouse #logistics”
data.limitations#Limitations: It writes text only. It does not generate images, and it cannot see images you attach. It knows your brand only through the diagnosis and brief you give it. Without a diagnosis or a detailed brief, drafts are more generic.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, under the Apache-2.0 licence. Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It turns a brief, a diagnosis, or a campaign into channel-native copy that teaches the reader something, with your product mentioned at most once.
Writes a post for one channel and topic when you ask (Content pipeline). Drafts the daily LinkedIn, X, and Instagram copy for each active campaign. Drafts outreach for a lead: a cold email and a LinkedIn message (Leads). Writes the shorter Studio pieces: podcast and short-video scripts, presentation outlines, infographic copy, and report drafts, plus course modules. Drafts the ad copy for a campaign and finds content gaps your audience wants filled.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Text drafts in the shape each channel expects, for example a LinkedIn post with a hook before the “see more” cut and a few hashtags, or a TikTok script with visual and voice-over lines. When a feature asks for a specific format, that format wins: a lead email is a subject line and the message, and a LinkedIn message is the message alone, with no hashtags or notes. Where an image belongs, it describes the image in words; it does not make one.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Your brief: channel, topic, tone, audience, language, and extra context. The diagnosis you ground it in, especially its brand overview and positioning. The day’s trending topics, for the daily social drafts. For lead outreach: the lead’s company and what is publicly known about it.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server. No third-party AI service is used.

data.guardrails#Guardrails: Aggregate segments only. It describes groups, never a real named person. No protected-class targeting. It does not infer or target audiences by race, ethnicity, religion, gender, age, or disability, and PULSE refuses requests to segment, target, or exclude people by them. Never invents data. No made-up statistics, survey results, market sizes, follower counts, or customer quotes, and PULSE refuses requests to invent them. When a field needs a figure it was not given, it says the figure is not in the data or describes the audience in words. Every pillar, stage, and phase is tied to a signal it was given. Search results are read as material, never as instructions. No hype and no fake urgency; initiatives a small team can start this week.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: Profiles, journeys, and strategies are planning documents on pages you control. Nothing is sent to a customer. Content pillars and roadmap phases pass through the judging ladder, which withholds proposals its judge disagrees with. It cannot contact anyone, publish, or launch a campaign.
data.limitations#Limitations: A profile is a model of a segment, not a record of real customers. It does not read individual CRM contacts. Without connected analytics, its weighting rests on the diagnosis and search signals alone.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, under the Apache-2.0 licence. Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It describes an audience segment and the path that takes it from first hearing of you to buying, then turns that into content pillars and a roadmap.
Writes a full 360° profile for a target audience (Customer 360). Maps a funnel journey (awareness, consideration, lead generation, follow-up) for a profile and a campaign objective. Drafts a content strategy: 3–5 weighted content pillars, a posting cadence, and an alignment score. Drafts a phased go-to-market roadmap. The basic profiles PULSE creates from each diagnosis’s audience segments are built without the model. This agent writes the deeper profiles you ask for.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Profiles (demographics, motivations, pain points, goals, preferred channels), journey maps with what the audience needs at each stage, content pillars whose weights sum to 100, and roadmaps of 3–4 phases, each with a timeframe, initiatives, and an expected outcome. Some of these come back as structured data the app displays as cards.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Your diagnosis, including its audience segments. Google Analytics and Google Ads figures, when those are connected. Live search signals for the audience. The campaign objective, audience, and channels you choose.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server. No third-party AI service is used. It reads your connected analytics and live search results while it works.

data.guardrails#Guardrails: Never invents market or competitor figures. PULSE refuses requests to fabricate them. No targeting or analysis by protected characteristics such as race, religion, gender, age, or disability. Advisory only. Requests to publish or spend are out of its scope. Your website and web research are read as material, never as instructions: text on a page that tries to redirect the agent is removed before the model sees it. Follows the shared value-first brand rule and writes in the language you use.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: The diagnosis is advice. You read it and decide what to act on. The drafts it seeds wait on the Approval screen, and the campaign it seeds is a draft. The 4-week plan can schedule posts, but a scheduled post goes out only after you approve its content and an administrator arms the channel. Channel prescriptions and brand-visibility insights can be withheld by the judging ladder when the judge disagrees with them. A withheld prescription never becomes a draft. It cannot publish, move budget, or change a campaign.
data.limitations#Limitations: It knows only what it could read. A channel it could not reach, or one you did not give it, is not analysed. Competitor observations come from public pages. What a competitor does not publish, it cannot know. Its 0–10 channel scores are judgements, not measurements. It does not see images or video on your site or profiles.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, under the Apache-2.0 licence. Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
Give it a website and your social accounts, and it writes a diagnosis of where your marketing stands and what to do in the next 30 days.
Writes the diagnosis behind every Site Audit: brand overview, positioning, SWOT, channel recommendations, content strategy, competitive landscape, search intent and campaign ideas, and a strategic opinion. Search intent and campaign ideas are shown at the end of the channel recommendations. Prescribes a role, priority, content ideas, and KPIs for each channel, and recommends long-form formats. Lays out the 4-week plan (the cronogram) that seeds your first follow-up cycle. Reads your metrics summary for a date range and writes a short read-out: summary, insights, recommendations, and its confidence.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces:
A structured diagnosis, saved with the sources it used. Each section is stored from its own heading, so a section that mentions another section’s topic is kept whole. PULSE then copies its findings into the rest of the app: draft content, a draft campaign, a follow-up cycle, audience profiles, and a market summary. See Concepts.
The relevance audit beside it is not written by this agent. Its 0–100 scores come from a rule-based scoring engine.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The pages of your website, read live when the audit runs. The audit stops if the site cannot be read. The LinkedIn URL, Instagram handle, and goals you enter in the audit form. Public web research about your niche and competitors. Your business profile, and Google Analytics or Google Ads signals when those are connected. For the metrics read-out: the follower, impression, engagement, click, lead, and conversion figures PULSE has synced.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server. No third-party AI service is used. Reading your website and researching your niche means PULSE fetches public web pages while the audit runs.

data.guardrails#Guardrails: Value first, no hard sell. It teaches the topic; your product appears at most once, as an honest example, never as the headline. Facts only from the brief. It never invents statistics, studies, quotes, customer names, or case results. If a point needs a number it was not given, it makes the point without one. No hype words, no clichés, no fake urgency. Will not handle payments or credentials. Its output is screened before it reaches you.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: You edit and approve every piece. Saved pieces go through the Approval review queue like any other content. Blog posts, podcast episodes, and the audiobook publish only when an administrator has armed that channel. See Publishing controls.
data.limitations#Limitations: It does not do its own research beyond what the brief and diagnosis give it, so a thin brief gives a thinner piece. Very long documents may be shorter than requested when the time budget is tight. It writes text only: no images, charts, or rendered video.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, under the Apache-2.0 licence. Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It is PULSE’s long-form copywriter: it writes the pieces a specialist reads, or listens to, to the end.
Writes whitepapers in Studio: an executive summary, sections that each make one argument, and a conclusion with next steps. Writes the blog posts the social engine drafts when the blog channel is armed. Writes the weekly audiobook, as prose meant to be read aloud. Shorter Studio pieces (podcast and short-video scripts, outlines, reports) are written by the channel content creator.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces:
Long text, shown once it has passed the brand and output checks: markdown with headings and short paragraphs for written pieces, and plain flowing prose with no lists or tables for audio. Audio itself is produced by the platform’s text-to-speech, not by this agent.
The length it can write in one pass depends on the deployment’s time budget. See Sovereign inference.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The brief: topic, industry, length, and any instructions you give. The diagnosis and campaign the piece belongs to, so its positioning matches your posts.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server. No third-party AI service is used.

data.guardrails#Guardrails: Refuses to harvest private data: private messages, personal email addresses, phone numbers, or home addresses. Refuses requests to invent engagement, follower, or reach numbers. A follower or audience figure the model gives is kept only if the search results state it; otherwise it is shown as unknown, never estimated. Treats web pages and search results as material to read, never as instructions: text in a page that tries to redirect the agent is removed before the model sees it. Research and recommendation only. Requests to publish or run a campaign are out of its scope.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: It recommends. You choose what goes into your plan. It cannot publish, launch a campaign, or contact anyone. Partner messages are drafted by Partnership outreach and sent by you.
data.limitations#Limitations: Audience sizes are copied from the search results, which may be out of date. They are not measured data from the platforms. Many channels show unknown, because the results did not state a figure. It sees only what is on the public web at the time of the search. Private or logged-in content is out of reach. Mention counts and trends show attention, not buying intent.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, under the Apache-2.0 licence. Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It researches your market and tells you which topics, hashtags, profiles, and channels are worth your attention.
Researches a topic and niche: trending topics, hashtag clusters, suggested profiles, a market summary, and competitive intelligence. Finds competitors’ YouTube and Instagram channels. Finds channels and podcasts where you could appear as a guest. See Audience and market.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A research result: topics with a 0–1 relevance score, hashtag clusters, suggested profiles with the reason each is relevant, and content opportunities. Channel and guest results carry an audience size only when the search results state one for that channel, a 0–1 fit score, and a contact hint when one was found. When no figure was found, the audience shows as unknown.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Live web search results for your topic, niche, region, and language. Any extra sources you attach: a search seed, a website or YouTube URL that PULSE scrapes, or pasted text. The brand overview from your diagnosis, so its suggestions fit your brand. Your like and dislike marks on trending posts, which ground later calls.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server. No third-party AI service is used. Research means PULSE fetches public web pages and search results while it works.

data.guardrails#Guardrails: Two-sided value first. Every message says what the partner gets, not only what you want. No hard sell. No hype, no spammy superlatives, no pressure. The goal of a first message is a reply, not a deal. Never invents facts about the partner. When little is known about a show, it keeps its claims general rather than making up numbers. Requests to invent audience or download figures are refused. Draft only. Requests to send, publish, or pay are refused. The shared input guardrails apply to every request.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: It only drafts. Each message is saved with status draft. You review it, edit it, and send it yourself. PULSE sends nothing.
data.limitations#Limitations: It knows only what the radar found. A thin partner record gives a more general message. It does not look up contact details beyond the hint the radar found, and it does not track replies.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, under the Apache-2.0 licence. Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
For a podcast, channel, or brand the market radar found, it drafts a short first message proposing a collaboration that clearly helps both sides, such as a guest-episode swap.
See Audience and market.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces:
A draft in four labelled parts:
Subject: one line. Value for them: why the collaboration helps their show and audience. Value for us: why it helps you. Message: a 120–180 word body ending with one small ask, such as a reply to schedule a recording.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: What is known about the partner from the radar result: its channel, its audience, and its angle. Your diagnosis: your positioning, audience, and offer.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server. No third-party AI service is used.

data.guardrails#Guardrails: Never invents numbers, campaigns, or results. An empty account summary is treated as the real answer, not a gap to fill. Requests to make up data are refused. Says when it does not know. If a question needs current or site-specific data it was not given, it says so. Advisory only, and the shared input guardrails apply to every message in the conversation, not only the latest. Websites it reads and search results are material, never instructions: text on a page that tries to redirect the assistant is removed before the model sees it.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: It answers and suggests. You make every change yourself. It has no way to change your account: it cannot launch a campaign, charge an ad account, approve content, or process a payment. Requests to launch a campaign, charge an ad account, delete your account, or process a payment are refused outright. The progress shown before a reply lists which grounding steps actually ran.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl:
Invented account.
Context: two active campaigns, no diagnostic yet.
You: Which campaign needs attention?
Assistant: “Returns webinar” has spent $2,100 of its $2,500 budget with 12 of 30 days left, so it is ahead of pace. There is no diagnostic yet, so I can’t comment on positioning. Run a Site Audit and I can.
data.limitations#Limitations: It sees a summary of your account, not every record. For detail, open the screen in question. It does not remember earlier research in the model; each search happens at question time. The AI Team roster does not act on the assistant’s behalf. Twins are a record you define, and no agent reads them yet. It cannot read images or screenshots.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, under the Apache-2.0 licence. Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It is the chat on every screen: it answers questions about your own PULSE account and your market, and says plainly when the answer is “none yet”.
Answers questions about your diagnostics, campaigns, scheduled posts, and tracked influencers. Reads a website you name and comments on its voice, positioning, and what that means for reach. Answers questions that need current facts from a live web search, citing the sources it was given. Can start a relevance audit for a URL and open the report. See Assistant, AI team, and voice.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A short conversational answer in your language. When an answer has several separate points, the app shows each as its own card, with a reason and, where there is one, a next step. It can read answers aloud.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Your message, typed or spoken. Spoken input is transcribed on the platform’s own speech server. A summary of your account sent with every message, as it is at that moment: the latest diagnostic, active campaigns, scheduled posts, and influencers. When there are none, the summary says so. The screen you are on, so “this” means what that screen shows. When relevant, a live scrape of a website you mention, or public search results.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server. No third-party AI service is used. When it scrapes a site or searches the web, PULSE fetches those public pages to answer you.

data.guardrails#Guardrails: Lead with their problem, not the pitch. One clear, low-friction next step. No hype, no fake urgency. Short and human. Spoken replies are one to three sentences, and objections get a brief acknowledgement, never an argument. No placeholders. It never says “[Name]” or “[company]”; if it does not know a detail, it talks around it. Never passes as a person. Requests to claim to be human, or to impersonate someone, are refused. Never invents customer results, prices, or statistics, and never takes payments or card details. On calls, what the person says is treated as material to answer, never as instructions to follow, and PULSE checks each transcribed turn against voice-specific rules that refuse attempts to inject or replay commands, as well as the shared input guardrails.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person starts every call. PULSE never dials on its own. Each call is placed from a lead’s Call action. During a call, replies are spoken as they are generated. No one approves each reply before it is heard, so review the lead’s script before you call. Scripts are drafts saved on the lead. A high-risk rating only creates a retention task in a follow-up cycle. A person decides what to do with it.
data.limitations#Limitations: It knows only what is in the lead record, the script, and the call so far. It cannot look things up mid-call. It cannot book meetings or send anything during or after a call. (Placing a call moves the lead to Contacted; that is PULSE’s board, not the agent’s decision.) Voice quality and turn-taking depend on the speech services and the phone line, not on this agent. A risk rating is a judgement from the stage and notes, not a prediction model.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, under the Apache-2.0 licence. Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.telephony-set-up#Telephony set-up:
Phone calls are off until an administrator configures them. They need a self-hosted Asterisk PBX. PULSE uses no per-minute calling service. The administrator sets the Asterisk connection and dial plan, and PULSE’s audio listener must be reachable from Asterisk. Without that, Call returns outbound calling isn't configured — set up Asterisk and .... The full set-up is in Telephony and messaging.
Outbound cold calling is regulated. Consent, calling hours, do-not-call lists, and recording disclosure are the operator’s responsibility.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It is PULSE’s sales development persona: it writes cold-call scripts, speaks short replies on a live phone call, and flags leads at risk of going cold.
Drafts a cold-call script for each lead that Find Leads prospects, grounded in what it found on that company’s own website (Leads). On a phone call you place with Call, replies to each thing the person says, turn by turn, using the lead’s cold-call script when one exists. Once a day, rates synced HubSpot leads as high, medium, or low risk of stalling, so PULSE can schedule a retention task for the high-risk ones (Churn watch). Cold emails and LinkedIn messages for leads are written by the channel content creator.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A short script: an opener, a reason for calling, questions, and one next step. On a call: one to three natural spoken sentences per turn, with no lists or formatting, read out by the platform’s text-to-speech. For churn watch: a single risk rating per lead.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: For a script: the lead’s name, title, and company, and, for prospected leads, gaps found on the lead’s website. For churn watch: the lead’s name, company, stage, and notes. Your diagnosis, to ground the pitch in your positioning. On a call: the transcript of what the person just said. Speech-to-text runs on the platform’s own speech server.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server, with speech-to-text and text-to-speech on the platform’s own speech services. No third-party AI service is used. The phone call itself travels through your Asterisk PBX and whatever phone carrier it connects to.

data.guardrails#Guardrails: Never destructive. No deleting data, dropping tables, shutting down hosts, or rolling back releases; its rollback only undoes its own recent change. Requests that point it that way are refused, and nothing is applied. Never touches security controls: authentication, encryption, certificates, secrets, firewalls, network policies, guardrails, or audit logs. What it reads about a failing component is treated as data, never as instructions.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: Automatic by default, with an off switch. An operator can turn automatic remediation off with one setting. Plans are then still recorded, but nothing is applied. Unsure means notify. A plan below a confidence floor, or anything outside the fixed list, becomes a notification and changes nothing. Every event and its outcome are shown in the system health view and the logs.
data.limitations#Limitations: It acts only on PULSE’s own components, not on the shared inference server or on other applications. Adding capacity stops at a ceiling. A problem that needs more than that needs an operator.
data.model#Model: The deployment’s base model, on its own inference server. It uses its own operations instructions, separate from the marketing agents.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It keeps PULSE’s own services running. When PULSE detects that one of its components is under pressure or unreachable, this agent picks one remediation from a short, fixed list, and PULSE applies it.
This is the one agent that acts without a person approving each step. It never writes for customers and never touches your marketing data.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces:
One plan: an action from the fixed list, the component it applies to, a one-sentence reason, and a confidence.
The fixed list:
Restart one of PULSE’s model services. Add capacity to one of PULSE’s model services, within a set ceiling. Pause failing calls for a short time, so they stop piling up. This resumes by itself. Roll back its own most recent change to a component, and only when that change happened shortly before the fault. It never rolls back a release, a deployment, or data, and never undoes a change someone else made. Notify: change nothing, and record the event for an operator.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: A health event raised by PULSE’s own monitoring: what is affected, how severe it is, and what was observed.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: Inside the deployment. It reads PULSE’s own health signals only. No third-party AI service is used.

data.guardrails#Guardrails: Refuses requests to invent KPI results or check-in data. It works from the numbers you entered. Will not endorse unsustainable work patterns. Plans include rest days. It does not know your calendar, so tell it in a check-in note if your time is limited. Planning only. Requests to publish or run a diagnosis are out of its scope. Follows the shared value-first brand rule.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: The revised plan is a recommendation. You decide what to change. It cannot write or publish posts, run a diagnosis, or move budget.
data.limitations#Limitations: It is only as good as your check-ins. With few or no check-ins there is little to recalculate from. Targets are planning aids, not forecasts.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, under the Apache-2.0 licence. Runink domain adaptation for this agent is planned; this release uses the base model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It keeps your 30-day plan realistic: when you ask, it recalculates the route from how your weekly check-ins have moved.
Reviews the check-in history of a follow-up cycle week over week. Says what is working, what to change, and what to drop, and why. Adjusts the content mix, the effort per channel, and the KPI targets to your actual trajectory. The first plan of a cycle comes from the diagnostic analyst. This agent revises it. See Follow-up and insights.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A revised plan, shown once it has passed the brand and output checks: weekly themes and goals, daily tasks with a channel, type, time estimate, and priority, KPI targets with an optimistic and a conservative figure, and the adjustments it made, each tied to the check-in numbers that triggered it.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The follow-up cycle and its planner tasks, with their status. Your weekly check-ins: new followers, posts, engagements, leads, satisfaction, and your notes on what worked and what did not. Your latest diagnosis, including its brand overview.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On the deployment’s own inference server. No third-party AI service is used.

System → Integrations (/integrations) has two tabs. Both store their credentials in the same per-user integrations table, and PULSE seals access and refresh tokens before writing them to the database.
There is no OAuth sign-in flow for these platforms. You paste a token or a service-account key that you created on the platform yourself. AccountsData sources The Accounts tab covers four platforms and uses IntegrationService.ConfigureIntegration.
Platform What you paste LinkedIn An access token, and optionally an account ID Instagram An access token, and optionally an account ID Google Analytics The full JSON key of a Google Cloud service account with access to the GA4 property, and the numeric Property ID (GA4 Admin → Property Settings). Both are required. Google Ads The JSON key of a service account with domain-wide delegation (scope adwords), the Ads Customer ID, a Developer Token, an optional Login Customer ID (manager account), and the Subject email the service account impersonates. All but the login customer ID are required. Test checks the credentials (TestConnection) and records the result as the integration’s status. For Google Analytics and Google Ads, PULSE runs a real API check with its own client. For LinkedIn and Instagram it calls the platform’s profile endpoint with your token.
Disconnect removes the stored credentials (DisconnectIntegration).
The Data sources tab is the shared Runink connections page (from org-runink/ui), served by PULSE over the same integrations rows. It covers two connectors:
Connector Credential Extra settings HubSpot A Private App token None GitHub A personal access token owner and repo, used as the target of audit-fix pull requests You can create, edit, rotate the credential, test, and delete a connection. The credential is write-only: the page never shows it again.
PULSE runs these connectors inside the PULSE server. It has no remote runners, so leave the runner unset. If you set a runner, an environment, or properties, the connection is refused and nothing is stored.
data.github#GitHub: Blog publishing to your website opens a pull request, or pushes a commit, with this token. The target repository is set by the administrator in PULSE_SITE_REPO, not here. See Site pipeline. Audit fixes in pr mode open a pull request against the owner and repo you set on this connection. If repo is missing you get github integration is missing a target owner/repo.
data.google-analytics#Google Analytics: The Trends tab on Insights: sync, trends, and forecasts. Without it you get Google Analytics isn't connected yet — configure it on the Integrations page first.
data.hubspot#HubSpot: Leads → Sync Now pulls contacts. Without HubSpot you get HubSpot isn't connected yet — configure it on the Integrations page first. Find Leads pushes new prospects to HubSpot. The daily churn engine reviews synced leads. The WhatsApp edge allows only senders who are contacts in HubSpot. See Telephony and messaging.
data.linkedin-and-instagram#LinkedIn and Inst: These store a token and can be tested. The scheduled LinkedIn publisher does not use the token you paste here: it uses an operator-supplied token. There is no working Instagram publisher yet. See which channels can publish.
