data:
PULSE is built around one loop. You audit a site, PULSE learns the market and audience from it, you create and approve content, and you publish and measure. Then the follow-up cycle feeds what you learned back into the next round.
This guide follows that loop in four stages. The stages are how these docs are organized. The app’s own navigation groups the same screens into five categories, shown in the table below.
1. AuditSite Audit: relevance scores, the diagnosis, and fixes you can apply. 2. Audience and marketRadar research, Customer 360, influencers, and partnerships. 2. LeadsSync, capture, prospect, write outreach, and call. 3. Content pipelineGenerate, review, approve, and schedule. 3. StudioWhitepapers, podcasts, shorts, presentations, and more. 4. Follow up and measure30-day cycles, check-ins, metrics, trends, and forecasts. Assistant, AI team, and voiceThe chat assistant, twins, and voice calls.
data.how-the-stages-connect#How the stages co:
One Site Audit seeds most of the other screens. When the diagnosis finishes, PULSE copies its findings forward, with no extra model calls:
From the diagnosis To Channel prescription suggestions Draft content on Approval, then Schedule once approved Prescriptions and audience segments A draft campaign on Campaigns The 4-week plan A 30-day cycle on Follow-up, with check-ins Audience segments Profiles on Customer 360 Competitive and positioning analysis A market summary for the Radar The niche Market research and up to five new leads, run in the background You can also start a stage on its own. Content, creatives, outreach, courses, Customer 360 profiles, and lead prospecting all accept an optional diagnostic_id that grounds the output in a diagnosis. They run without one.
data.languages#Languages: The app ships English, Spanish, French, and Portuguese catalogs. Pick the interface language in Settings. Generated content has its own language, set on each generation request.
data.where-each-screen-lives#Where each scree: Navigation category Screens Overview Overview (dashboard), Marketing Console, Site Audit, Insights, Impact Analytics, Content Gaps Audience Influencers, Customer 360, Persona Profile, Intelligence Console, Leads, Follow-up Content Campaigns, Creatives, Approval, Schedule, Courses Studio Content Strategy, Strategy Roadmap, Whitepapers, Podcasts, Shorts, Presentations, Infographics, Reports System Integrations, AI Team, Settings, Billing Your avatar opens Account. Administrators also see Admin. The old /metrics and /analytics addresses redirect to Insights.

data.ai-team-twins#AI Team (twins):
System → AI Team (/twins) is a roster of twins. A twin has a name, a role, a system prompt, and optionally an avatar (TwinService.CreateTwin). New twins start active. You can pause one and activate it again (UpdateTwinStatus).
Today the roster is a record of the twins you define. No backend agent reads it yet, so a twin does not act on its own.
data.talk-instead-of-typing#Talk instead of t: Voice input. The microphone records a clip and uploads it to /voice/transcribe. Speech-to-text runs on the platform’s Voxtral server. Spoken replies. The assistant can read answers aloud through ModelService.SynthesizeSpeech. Speech synthesis runs inside PULSE. Both voice endpoints require you to be signed in.
data.the-assistant#The assistant:
The assistant is a floating chat available on every screen. It sends your messages to ModelService.Complete with the assistant agent and streams the answer back. It can also start a relevance audit for a URL and open the full report.
Everything it says comes from the platform’s own model. Nothing goes to an outside AI service.
data.voice-calls-with-the-assistant#Voice cal:
The full-screen call view (/call) negotiates a WebRTC call through /voice/webrtc/offer. PULSE only relays the signaling. The call itself is carried by the platform’s shared calling agent, which the deployment names in CALLING_AGENT_URL. When that is not set, the offer is refused with HTTP 503 rather than connecting a call that carries no audio.
Phone calls to leads are different. They go through Asterisk. See Leads.

data: These screens answer two questions: what is happening in your market, and who you are talking to.
data.competitors-and-guest-spots#Competitors: DiscoverCompetitorChannels finds competitors’ YouTube and Instagram channels by web search. Give it competitor names, or let it derive them from the niche. DiscoverGuestOpportunities finds YouTube channels and podcasts you could appear on as a guest, for a topic you choose. Each result carries an estimated audience size, a 0–1 fit score, and a contact hint when one was found.
data.customer-360#Customer 360:
Audience → Customer 360 lists one profile per audience segment of your diagnoses. PULSE builds them from each segment’s roles, areas, and technologies, without calling the model.
To go deeper:
GenerateProfile streams a full 360° profile for a target audience, from a diagnosis, optionally for specific channels. GenerateJourneyMap streams a multi-stage funnel map, with recommended content, for a profile and a campaign objective such as brand_awareness or lead_gen. Audience → Intelligence Console is a workspace for the same profile generation, with the persona streaming into an output panel as it is written. Persona Profile lists the personas generated so far.
data.influencers#Influencers: Audience → Influencers is a simple list of people you track. Add one with a name, handle, platform, a score, and notes (InfluencerService.SaveInfluencer). PULSE does not fetch follower data for this list.
data.partnership-outreach#Partnership outreac: DraftPartnershipOutreach streams a first-contact message for a discovered channel. It proposes an exchange that benefits both sides and states what each side gets. It only drafts. The message is staged with status draft, and nothing is sent. Find drafts again with ListPartnershipOutreach.
data.radar-market-research#Radar: market rese: The Radar sits in the Market tab of a Site Audit result. A finished diagnosis gives it a starting market summary, so it does not open empty.
data.research-a-topic#Research a topic:
RadarService.StartResearch streams findings for a topic and niche. You can narrow it by channel, target audience, region (for example BR or US), and language (for example pt-BR).
You can attach extra sources to ground the research beyond the default web search:
Source kind What PULSE does with it Web search seed Runs the query live Website or YouTube URL Scrapes it on the server Pasted text Uses the text as given A result holds trending topics (each with a 0–1 relevance score), hashtag clusters, suggested profiles, a market summary, and competitive intelligence.
data.trending-posts#Trending posts: GetTrendingPosts returns real scraped posts for a niche, each with an image, its source, and a 0–100 hot score. Mark a post like or dislike (SubmitPostFeedback). Your reactions feed the grounding of later trending-post calls. Profile-level feedback (useful, not_relevant, save, block) is a separate call, UseRadarFeedback.

data:
Content moves through four steps: generate, review, schedule, and publish. Every piece is a Content row with a status, so you can always see where it is.
Status Meaning DRAFT Created, not yet ready for review PENDING_REVIEW Waiting on the Approval screen APPROVED Approved for publication REJECTED Rejected, with the reviewer’s reason PUBLISHED Published by a publisher ARCHIVED Archived
data.campaigns#Campaigns:
Content → Campaigns (/campaigns) groups content under an objective (brand_awareness, lead_gen, engagement, or sales), channels, a budget, a currency, dates, and an audience. You can create, update, archive, and delete campaigns (CampaignService). Deleting is a soft delete.
A campaign’s status is one of DRAFT, ACTIVE, PAUSED, COMPLETED, and ARCHIVED. The daily engines work only on active campaigns, so activate a campaign to start its daily drafts, documents, and episodes.
data.creatives#Creatives:
Content → Creatives (/creatives) holds the media attached to content and campaigns.
CreateCreative registers an asset you already have: an image prompt, a video script, alt text, dimensions. GenerateCreative generates media and saves it as a creative. It makes video only. Still-image generation was retired, and a still-image request returns Unimplemented: still-image generation is not available: the image-generation tier was retired. For video, pick a platform preset: youtube, youtube_shorts, instagram_reel, instagram_feed, or instagram_story. The preset sets the resolution and frame rate. You can set the number of scenes (1–100), the frame rate (12–60, default 30), an avatar, a voice, and a target language. Video needs the video tool the deployment configures (BINARY_VIDEO_CLI).
Generated files are stored sealed on the server and served from /creatives/ and /media/, only to a signed-in owner or through a link the server signed.
data.generate#Generate:
Content reaches review from three places:
A Site Audit. Each channel prescription’s suggestions become drafts. You. ContentService.GenerateContent streams a post for one channel and topic. You can set the tone (professional, casual, bold, or educational; the default is professional), audience, language, extra context, a campaign, and a diagnosis to ground it in. The result is saved and goes to review when generation finishes. The social engine. Once a day it drafts a LinkedIn post, an X thread, and an Instagram caption for each active campaign, grounded in that day’s trending topics. They wait for review like everything else. Studio pieces (whitepapers, podcasts, and the rest) can be saved as content with SaveGeneratedContent, so they can be approved and scheduled too. See Studio.
data.review-on-approval#Review on Approval:
Content → Approval (/approval) is a swipe-style review queue.
Edit changes the title, body, hashtags, or call to action (UpdateContent). The item stays pending. Approve marks it approved (ApproveContent). Reject marks it rejected and keeps your reason (RejectContent). When you approve a piece whose channel has a publisher, PULSE tries to publish it right away. That happens only if the channel is armed. An approval is consent to the content, not to the channel, and there is no override. See Publishing controls.
data.schedule#Schedule:
Content → Schedule (/publishing) lists the queue and lets you schedule approved content. Pick the content, a channel, and a date and time (PublishingService.SchedulePost). The screen offers LinkedIn, Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, and Blog.
Every 30 seconds the publishing worker dispatches posts that are due. Each row ends in one of these states:
Status Meaning pending Waiting for its time publishing Being dispatched now posted Published withheld The channel was disarmed when the post came due. This is final: re-arming does not replay old posts. Schedule the content again to re-queue it. failed The dispatch was tried and failed, for example a dead token or a platform quota error Every row also carries a reason and a reason_status. A withheld or failed row with no recorded reason shows reason_status: missing, never a blank.
data.which-channels-can-actually-publish#Whic: Channel Publisher Blog A Hugo post on your own website, through GitHub. See Site pipeline. LinkedIn A text-only post on one personal profile. Company pages are not supported. YouTube A real upload. Visibility comes from YOUTUBE_PRIVACY_STATUS, and defaults to private. Podcast Inclusion in the podcast RSS feed. Platforms poll the feed. Book outline (audiobook) The same feed, as its own channel Instagram No working publisher yet. The uploader is a stub. Facebook, X, TikTok, email No publisher. A dispatch fails with no publishing integration for channel ... yet.

data: The last stage closes the loop. You work through a 30-day plan, report how each week went, and let PULSE recalculate the route. Then you check the numbers.
data.follow-up-cycles#Follow-up cycles:
Audience → Follow-up (/followup) tracks one 30-day cycle at a time. A Site Audit creates the first one from its 4-week plan, with one planner task per entry.
GetCycleProgress shows the current cycle: its number, the current week (1–4), tasks done out of total, and the prescription summary. Pass no cycle ID to get the active cycle. GetPlanner returns the tasks for one week, or all weeks with week_number 0. Each task has a day, a channel, a content type (post, story, reel, article, engagement), and a due date. UpdateTaskStatus moves a task to TODO, IN_PROGRESS, DONE, SKIPPED, or BLOCKED.
data.impact-analytics-and-content-gaps#Impact:
Overview → Impact Analytics shows the metrics summary and the daily evolution chart, with the same data caveat as the Metrics tab.
Overview → Content Gaps runs InsightsService.AnalyzeContentGaps when you ask for it. You can narrow it with a focus area and a date range. It returns the topics and formats your audience wants but you under-serve. Each gap has a 0–100 demand score, a coverage score, and an opportunity score, plus a rationale. The response also has an overall coverage index. Gaps pass through the judging ladder.
data.metrics-tab#Metrics tab:
Reads MetricsService: a KPI summary, a daily time series, a per-channel breakdown, and an agent reading, which is the model’s interpretation of the current numbers with key insights and recommendations.
Nothing in PULSE writes per-channel social metrics yet. The KPI summary reads followers, impressions, engagements, clicks, leads, and reach from a metrics table that no connector fills, so those figures stay at zero. The count of published content is real: it is counted from your content. Campaign filtering is not supported, because metrics are not stored per campaign.
data.recalculate-the-route#Recalculate the ro: RecalculateWithEvolution streams a revised plan for the cycle, based on how the check-ins evolved. GetEvolutionHistory returns the check-in history across cycles with a written trend analysis.
data.trends-tab#Trends tab:
Reads AnalyticsService, which works from Google Analytics 4. Connect Google Analytics first. See Connections.
SyncGaData pulls one GA4 metric’s daily values into a local cache. Use the GA4 API name, for example sessions, activeUsers, or conversions. It looks back 90 days by default. GetTrends reads the cached series. GetForecast forecasts the next 14 days by default, with a band of plus or minus two residual standard deviations. It also lists anomalies, changepoints, and any detected seasonality. It runs on the cache, so it works even when Google Analytics is unreachable. A forecast needs at least four days of synced data. With fewer you get not enough synced GA data to forecast (N days, need at least 4) — sync more history first.
data.weekly-check-in#Weekly check-in: SaveCheckIn records a week: new followers, posts published, engagements, leads, a 1–10 satisfaction score, and three free-text fields for what happened, what did not work, and what worked.

data: Audience → Leads (/leads) is a sales board with five columns: New, Contacted, Qualified, Won, and Lost. Leads arrive four ways, and each card can draft outreach, place a call, or move to another column.
data.call-a-lead#Call a lead:
Call places a real outbound phone call (CallLead). An AI voice agent handles the conversation, and the lead moves to Contacted.
This needs a self-hosted Asterisk PBX that an administrator has configured. See Telephony and messaging. Without it you get outbound calling isn't configured — set up Asterisk and ..., naming the missing settings. A lead with no phone number returns lead has no phone number.
Outbound cold calling is regulated: consent, calling hours, do-not-call lists, and recording disclosure. Check the rules that apply to you before you dial real numbers.
data.churn-watch#Churn watch: Once a day, the predictive churn engine reviews synced HubSpot leads for churn risk and schedules retention tasks for high-risk ones. They appear as a follow-up cycle named “Predictive Churn Retention Cycle”.
data.draft-outreach#Draft outreach:
Draft writes a personalized message for one lead (GenerateOutreach) and streams it as it is written. Pick the channel:
Channel Output email A cold email with a subject line call_script A cold-call script linkedin_dm A LinkedIn direct message You can also set a tone (professional, casual, bold, consultative), a language, extra context, and a diagnosis to ground the pitch. Drafts are saved per lead (ListOutreach). PULSE does not send them.
data.find-new-leads-on-the-web#Find new leads:
Find Leads asks for a niche (for example “logistics SaaS”), an optional region, and optionally a diagnosis to ground the outreach. It streams progress as it works:
A headless-browser search finds candidate company and directory pages. PULSE crawls each page for emails, phone numbers, company names, and LinkedIn links. It skips system mailboxes, form placeholders, list vendors, and free consumer mail domains. For each prospect it drafts a cold-call script, an email, and a social DM. It saves the leads and, if HubSpot is connected, pushes them to HubSpot. The default is 10 leads per run, and the maximum is 25. Without HubSpot, the leads are still saved locally and the progress log says so.
data.move-a-lead#Move a lead: Move changes the column (UpdateLeadStage). The valid stages are new, contacted, qualified, won, and lost. Anything else is refused with invalid pipeline stage.
data.sync-from-hubspot#Sync from HubSpot:
HubSpot is the only CRM PULSE syncs today. Connect it first under Integrations → Data sources. See Connections.
PULSE keeps a thin local copy of each contact. It shows HubSpot’s own lifecycle stage as-is and does not score leads itself. The board column is PULSE’s own pipeline_stage, separate from HubSpot’s lifecycle stage.
data.where-leads-come-from#Where leads come f: Source How source value HubSpot Sync Now pulls contacts from your connected HubSpot account (SyncLeads) hubspot By hand Add lead (CreateLead). A lead needs at least a name, an email, or a company. manual by default Web prospecting Find Leads searches the public web for a niche (ScrapeLeads) scraped A Site Audit A finished diagnosis prospects up to five leads for its niche in the background scraped

data:
Site Audit is where the loop starts. One URL goes in. Two analyses come out:
The diagnosis, written by the model: positioning, SWOT, competitive landscape, channel recommendations, a content strategy, and a 4-week plan. The relevance audit, computed by a rule-based scoring engine: nested 0–100 scores with the fixes that would raise them.
data.apply-the-fixes#Apply the fixes:
Each audit returns actions: concrete fix artifacts such as a robots.txt, a canonical tag, a JSON-LD block, or a rewritten title. Each action says where it goes, how confident PULSE is, and whether it is safe to apply automatically.
On the report, enter the path of a local checkout of your site and choose a mode:
Mode Effect plan Dry run. Lists the file changes. No side effects. Always allowed. apply Writes the files into the repository on the server’s filesystem. commit Writes and commits, on branch seo/pulse-remediation by default. pr Opens a pull request. data.fill-in-the-form#Fill in the form:
Open Overview → Site Audit (/site-audit). Enter:
Website URL (required). LinkedIn URL and Instagram Handle (optional). Your goals. The choices are Improve SEO & Relevance, Grow Audience & Market, Generate & Manage Leads, Drive Sales & Campaigns, Deepen Customer Insights, Automate Follow-ups, and Streamline Workflows.
data.read-the-result#Read the result: The result page (/site-audit/result) has five tabs: Overview, Strategy, SEO, Market, and Action Plan. It also runs the relevance audit for the same URL. Past audits are under View History (/site-audit/history).
data.run-it#Run it:
Choose Run Site Audit. The app creates the diagnostic record (CreateDiagnostic) and then streams the analysis (GenerateDiagnostic).
PULSE reads your website first. If it cannot, the diagnosis stops with could not read (...) — a reachable website with readable content is required to run the diagnostic.
While it runs, the progress list shows what the backend actually did, for example “Grounded diagnosis in the scraped page content”. These entries are recorded by the backend, not claimed by the model, and they stay on the diagnosis afterwards as agent_tasks. The sources it read are kept as sources_used.
data.the-relevance-audit#The relevance audit:
The scoring engine is config-driven. Almost every check is a rule; one content check asks the model. It scores nine composites. The default weights come from internal/scoring/default_config.json:
Composite Default weight AI Visibility 0.30 Search Visibility 0.25 Technical Foundation 0.20 Authority & Trust 0.20 Acquisition 0.15 Monetization 0.10 Engagement 0.10 Retention 0.10 Demographics 0.05 Scores nest: check, then signal, then composite, then overall. Each composite also reports its coverage, the share of its weight that was actually scored. A 90 at 0.4 coverage means much less than a 90 at 1.0. Checks that need a data source you have not configured are skipped, and their weight is spread over the rest instead of counting as zero. The report lists those sources in skipped_data_sources.
Add two or three competitor URLs to switch the benchmark checks into relative mode. A profile changes the weights. The shipped profiles are ai-focused and authority-focused.
Open the full report at /site-audit/report.
data.what-happens-after-it-finishes#What happ:
PULSE copies the findings into the rest of the app. This runs once per diagnosis, even if you regenerate it:
Draft posts on Approval, from the channel prescriptions. One draft campaign on Campaigns, linked to the diagnosis. A 30-day cycle on Follow-up, one planner task per cronogram entry. Scheduled posts for the cronogram’s channels. They publish only on armed channels. See Publishing controls. One profile per audience segment on Customer 360. A market summary and background market research for the Radar. Up to five leads prospected from the public web, in the background.
data.what-the-diagnosis-contains#What the dia: Part What it is Positioning, SWOT, competitive landscape, AI opinion Free-text analysis sections Channel prescriptions Per channel: its role, priority, content ideas, CTA style, and KPIs Document prescriptions Recommended long-form formats, with ideas Brand visibility How to be found and cited by AI search engines, with target terms and actions Audience segments Tiers such as decision makers and end users, with their roles and technologies Cronogram A week-by-week, channel-by-channel task plan Channel prescriptions and brand-visibility insights pass through the judging ladder. A proposal the judge disagrees with is withheld from these lists.

data: The Studio category holds the long-form and planning generators. They are all streaming calls, so text appears as the model writes it. Long pieces can take tens of minutes on CPU.
data.audio-and-video-from-the-background-engi:
Finished audio and video come from background engines, not from the Studio screens. They run on active campaigns:
Engine Output How it publishes Podcast engine Episodes, scripted and synthesized to WAV Staged for review; published by inclusion in the podcast feed Audiobook engine A weekly long-form book The same feed, as its own channel Shorts engine Short videos Staged as a YouTube upload. Refuses to start when the image has no video tool. Document engine Documents Daily, for review Speech is synthesized by Runink TIDE’s shared ttsd service. Publishing each of these depends on its channel being armed. See Publishing controls.
data.content-strategy#Content Strategy: Studio → Content Strategy calls InsightsService.GenerateContentStrategy with an objective (for example “Thought Leadership” or “Lead Gen”), channels, and an audience. It returns content pillars, each with example topics and a recommended share of the mix, a posting cadence, a 0–100 alignment score, and a summary.
data.courses-and-avatars#Courses and avatars:
Content → Courses calls CourseService.GenerateCourse with a topic and a number of modules. For each module the model writes a lesson title, a teaching script, and a quiz grounded in that script.
If you pass an avatar and the deployment can generate video, each module also gets a video. If it cannot, the module is saved with no video, not a placeholder, and the server logs why.
Avatars come from AvatarService.CreateAvatar: a name, a photo, and optionally a voice sample, both base64-encoded.
data.long-form-writing#Long-form writing:
Screen Call You provide You get Whitepapers GenerateWhitepaper Topic, industry, length (short, medium, in-depth) A long-form document Podcasts GeneratePodcast Source material, host style (conversational, deep_dive, news), target minutes A podcast script Shorts GenerateShorts Topic, platform (youtube, instagram), visual style A short-video script with visual cues and on-screen text Presentations GeneratePresentation Objective, slide count, brand colors A slide-by-slide outline Infographics GenerateInfographic Data source, layout (timeline, comparison, process) Infographic copy: title, data points, icon ideas Reports GenerateReport Timeframe, metrics to highlight, export format A report draft These screens produce text. The podcast and shorts screens write scripts; they do not record audio or render video. A report is written by the model from the timeframe and metric names you give it. It does not read your metrics, and the export format is a hint in the prompt, not a file conversion.
The whitepaper generator is the most grounded. It uses the long-form copywriter agent, injects the same diagnosis context that content generation uses, and says so when it has none instead of inventing facts. Its length setting sets a real token budget.
To approve or schedule a Studio piece, save it as content with ContentService.SaveGeneratedContent.
data.strategy-roadmap#Strategy Roadmap:
Studio → Strategy Roadmap calls GenerateStrategyRoadmap with an objective and a planning horizon in weeks. It returns phases (for example “Foundation”, “Momentum”, “Scale”), each with a timeframe, initiatives, projected momentum, and an outcome, plus a 0–100 readiness score.
Both are grounded in your diagnosis, your published content, and live market signals, and both run through the judging ladder. A pillar or phase the judge disagrees with is withheld.
